video_title: Gold, Market Flows, AI & the Next Investing Regime | Protect the Pile Episode 24
gist: A Hedgeye 'Protect the Pile' panel (host Patrick Kent with PMs Sam Ramen and Brooks Cutright, joined by thematic/family-office investor Jerry Jordan) argues current markets are driven far more by quant flows, buybacks and leverage than fundamentals, with record valuations and AI-capex-inflated earnings masking rising risk. They build a dollar-debasement/yield-curve-control thesis favoring gold over US equities, debate AI model commoditization ahead of possible Anthropic/OpenAI IPOs, flag an under-appreciated energy supply squeeze, and warn of hidden leverage in private-equity-owned insurers.

insights.claim: Quant/systematic trading firms Jane Street, Citadel, De Shaw and Renaissance together account for roughly 60% of daily trading volume, meaning markets are now driven far more by mechanical flow than by fundamental analysis.
insights.speaker: Jerry Jordan, guest
insights.so_what: Fundamentals matter less day-to-day than positioning and flow; investors should weight technical/flow signals alongside valuation work.
insights.quote: Citadel, Jane Street, De Shaw, Renaissance, they're 60% of the trading volume. I mean, it's it's bananas.

insights.claim: Contrary to the popular narrative that passive index flows (roughly $200-500 billion/year) are the dominant force distorting markets, corporate buybacks (~$1 trillion/year, concentrated in the ~25 largest index constituents) are the bigger driver of index returns.
insights.speaker: Jerry Jordan, guest
insights.so_what: Investors worried about passive-flow distortion may be focused on the wrong culprit; track buyback pace and concentration as the more important index-return driver.
insights.quote: buybacks alone are a trillion... I think the buybacks are much more likely to drive the index returns than the passive drip drip drip flow is to drive the index returns.

insights.claim: Institutional portfolio turnover has exploded to the point where trillions of dollars now turn over three times a week with no tax sensitivity, versus the 25-30%/year turnover that used to draw consultant scrutiny; in this regime, price action itself is effectively the dominant factor, overwhelming traditional multi-factor models.
insights.speaker: Jerry Jordan, guest
insights.so_what: Multi-factor valuation models are secondary to pure price/momentum signals in the current structure, explaining why momentum-chasing dominates.
insights.quote: I always joke that when people talk about their 40 or 50 or 100 factor model, I always say that's great, but price is 99 of a hundred of the factors and everything else is subservient to that.

insights.claim: Because investors are heavily shorting cap-weighted mega-caps (Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Nvidia) against higher-beta stock-picking books, headline index performance looks deceptively smooth while dispersion and damage among individual, higher-beta names underneath is severe.
insights.speaker: Brooks Cutright, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Index-level calm is masking real risk-off action; single-stock and style dispersion, not the index level, is the better real-time risk gauge right now.
insights.quote: the amount of of shorting of Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Nvidia, like against your your higher beta picks is, in my estimation, one of the reasons why the the tape just hasn't really seen any aggressive selloff.

insights.claim: Heavily levered hedge funds (4-10x leverage) rapidly de-lever and re-lever in response to small intraday P&L swings (e.g., a book down only 75bps triggers a forced unwind), producing self-reinforcing rallies where the lowest-quality, most-shorted stocks all surge together purely from short covering and deleveraging rather than fundamentals.
insights.speaker: Jerry Jordan, guest
insights.so_what: Sharp, indiscriminate rallies in weak or heavily-shorted names are often mechanical deleveraging noise rather than fundamental repricing, and should not be chased.
insights.quote: there's a risk manager sitting on a desk somewhere who goes over and taps the trader's shoulder and says, 'your fund is down 75 bips today because of this V blowout on your 26 longs versus 26 shorts. Uh, unwind it.'

insights.claim: Passive index rebalancing itself moves roughly $1 trillion a year and has its own seasonal pattern, including an annual-adjustment-driven growth-outperforms-value tendency around September that investors should be aware of alongside the buyback-driven flows.
insights.speaker: Brooks Cutright, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: The September passive-rebalancing window is a systematic, dated flow event that can be positioned around independent of fundamentals.
insights.quote: the the seasonality and the the systemization of of the passive getting rebalanced is about a trillion dollars a year, too... we're getting into the the September cycle when you when you find growth outperform value.

insights.claim: A 35-year veteran thematic/family-office investor has cut his developed-market (especially US) equity weighting well below the typical 25-30% range because of record valuations, record and likely unsustainable profit margins, and an unprecedented consensus belief that markets must always go up.
insights.speaker: Jerry Jordan, guest
insights.so_what: A veteran manager running well below typical equity exposure signals that sentiment and valuation extremes warrant defensive positioning even inside a bullish-trend tape.
insights.quote: We've got a belief in markets that honestly I've never seen in my in doing this for 35 years. I've never seen the amount of people who believe that the market has to go up year after year.

insights.claim: Corporate profit margins are at record highs and, per most quant research, margins are the most mean-reverting metric in markets, implying the current margin level is an unsustainable tailwind to earnings.
insights.speaker: Jerry Jordan, guest
insights.so_what: Forward earnings estimates that assume margin persistence are vulnerable; watch for margin mean-reversion as an earnings risk.
insights.quote: We have certainly record margins which I think are unsustainable and most quants will tell you the most mean reverting thing out there is margins.

insights.claim: Investors who bought Europe, Latin America, or Asia ex-Japan in 2007 didn't recover their capital until 2021-22, enduring roughly 40% drawdowns every three years along the way; the US market could plausibly face a similar multi-decade stretch of volatility without net price progress.
insights.speaker: Jerry Jordan, guest
insights.so_what: A long US equity flat/volatile regime is a real scenario to hedge against rather than assuming buy-the-dip always works over a normal time horizon.
insights.quote: I think we're staring at what Europe did for the last 20 years which is a lot of up and down and no price progress.

insights.claim: From 2000-2003, equal-weight indices outperformed cap-weight by 40-50%, yet equal-weight still fell about 30% over that period, meaning the outperformance came entirely from declining less, not from gaining.
insights.speaker: Jerry Jordan, guest
insights.so_what: Given today's top-heavy index concentration, tilting toward equal weight is a way to reduce, not eliminate, downside in a valuation unwind.
insights.quote: if we look back at 2000 from 2000 to 2003 equal weight outperformed cap cap weight by 40 or 50% over that time period, it still went down 30%.

insights.claim: Roughly half of Q2 earnings growth at big hyperscaler/platform companies came from mark-ups on their private AI investments rather than operating results — about 25 of the 45 percentage points of growth, not the ~3% many assume.
insights.speaker: Jerry Jordan, guest
insights.so_what: Reported hyperscaler earnings quality is weaker than headline growth implies; strip out unrealized private-investment gains when valuing these names.
insights.quote: half of their earnings growth in the second quarter came from the pricing of their private investments... not 3% of the 45, but 25 of the 45.

insights.claim: Markets are repeating the classic mistake of putting a peak multiple on peak (cyclical/commodity) earnings in commodity semiconductors and energy names — commodity chips like Micron should trade around 4x earnings at the cycle top and 28x at the trough, the opposite of how retail is currently treating them as 'cheap.'
insights.speaker: Jerry Jordan, guest
insights.so_what: Low headline P/Es on cyclical semis and energy names may be a value trap rather than genuine cheapness, especially with retail (25% of volume) chasing them.
insights.quote: Micron should trade at four times earnings at the top and it should trade at 28 times earnings at the bottom or or times, you know.

insights.claim: If 'intelligence is the new electricity,' hyperscalers' AI businesses increasingly resemble capital-intensive utilities earning roughly 4% ROIC rather than the ~30%+ ROIC historically generated by software/cloud businesses.
insights.speaker: Brooks Cutright, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Justifies caution on hyperscaler AI-capex narratives; watch ROIC trends, not just revenue growth, in AI infrastructure spend.
insights.quote: if you said intelligence is the new electricity well then these are utilities and that's a 4% ROIC um not a 34% ROIC.

insights.claim: Each new generation of AI chips has meaningfully lowered token-production cost per watt, and further networking/data-center configuration efficiency gains remain available before hitting a power or chip-productivity ceiling, supporting improving AI margins over the medium term.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Argues against the bear case on AI unit economics — margin improvement from chip and network efficiency gains is a real, ongoing tailwind, not yet exhausted.
insights.quote: every new generation of chips has low cost um token production per watt... every chip generation has done that.

insights.claim: AI providers reportedly sell roughly $8,000 worth of compute for about $200 a month, raising doubt about whether the business can scale to profitability without ongoing subsidization from the roughly $2 trillion capex wave currently rippling through chipmakers and cloud infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: If AI unit economics fail to close, the earnings/margin boost currently flowing through chipmakers and cloud providers from this capex wave could reverse sharply.
insights.quote: you're selling me $8,000 of compute for $200. Like of course it looks like it's massively productivity enhancing.

insights.claim: Frontier AI models are likely to follow an 80/20 dynamic similar to smartphones (Apple vs. Samsung): most of the profit will concentrate in the top one or two frontier models (Anthropic, OpenAI) while most usage volume spreads across cheaper lagging and open-weight models.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Investors should expect profit concentration at the top of the AI model stack even as unit volumes commoditize below it — favoring frontier-model leaders over the broader field.
insights.quote: all the profit is in these two front-end models, but all the volume and activity is going to be in lesser models... lagging models, open weight models, it's going to be all there.

insights.claim: Large language models are commoditizing as 7-10 well-capitalized global players all treat AI as an existential threat and converge on similar model quality; Meta and possibly SpaceX are candidates to become the lowest-cost-producer survivors in what is becoming a commodity-style model market, with stickiness coming from ecosystem lock-in and flat-price multi-year deals rather than model superiority.
insights.speaker: Jerry Jordan, guest
insights.so_what: Favor the eventual lowest-cost model producers and ecosystem-lock-in plays over paying up for perceived model-quality leadership, which is expected to compress.
insights.quote: the large language models are are all commoditizing... as we know with commodity markets, you know, the lowest cost provider always wins or or or survives at the very least survives.

insights.claim: A reported 70% of certain startups (cited from Y Combinator-type statistics) are already using free or cheap Chinese open-source LLMs to conserve cash, which creates a latent data-security 'reckoning' risk once companies realize their proprietary data has been exposed to the same foreign model shared by competitors.
insights.speaker: Jerry Jordan, guest
insights.so_what: A future data-security scandal tied to Chinese open-source model adoption by cash-strapped startups is an under-priced tail risk worth watching.
insights.quote: I've read statistics that say a lot of the startups being um being invested in by like, you know, Y Combinator, etc., 70% of them are using the essentially free Chinese models.

insights.claim: Expect a structural shift toward proprietary small language models (SLMs) built and housed inside large enterprises (e.g., GE, Cisco, JPMorgan) on their own data plus AWS/Azure infrastructure, which could in aggregate become a larger market over time than the frontier hyperscaler/LLM providers, while still requiring substantial ongoing infrastructure investment.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Enterprise-proprietary SLM infrastructure spend is a second, potentially larger AI investment theme beyond the frontier-model hyperscaler race, supporting continued cloud/infra capex regardless of which model layer wins.
insights.quote: there's going to be an explosion a proliferation of not LLMs but SLM small language models that are going to be all proprietary... probably going to be larger over time than what these guys are doing here.

insights.claim: Amazon may be taking the smarter strategic path by abandoning ambitions to build its own frontier model and instead becoming a hyperscaler-agnostic, multi-model supplier, positioning at the customer-data layer where value could accrue from being infrastructure- and model-neutral rather than locked into one model provider.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: A model-agnostic, data-layer positioning strategy (like Amazon's) could be a more durable competitive position than owning a proprietary frontier model.
insights.quote: Amazon's now taking the better approach to this by sort of getting rid of any idea of doing their own model and being a multimodel kind of supplier.

insights.claim: A potential Anthropic or OpenAI IPO/S-1 filing could become one of the most consequential financial documents in the past decade because it will finally reveal true AI unit economics, creating real risk of pricking the AI-driven equity bubble sometime in the roughly two-and-a-half months before the November midterms.
insights.speaker: Brooks Cutright, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Watch the timing of an Anthropic or OpenAI IPO filing as a binary catalyst event for AI-related equities and broader market risk appetite.
insights.quote: their their S1 is probably going to be like one of the most consequential financial documents in the past 10 years.

insights.claim: Expect the Anthropic S-1 to surprise markets positively given its unprecedented growth speed and strong profitability metrics, while OpenAI is unlikely to IPO within the current calendar year and will look weaker by comparison — making Anthropic's filing effectively the 'peak AI' moment.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: A bullish, contrarian call ahead of an expected Anthropic listing — positions it as a positive catalyst rather than the bubble-pricking risk others expect.
insights.quote: I actually think that the S1's going to surprise the the Jesus out of people in a positive way... I think that's probably going to be peak AI.

themes.theme: Dollar Debasement, Bessent & the Path to Yield Curve Control

insights.claim: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, fresh off intervening in the yen, is now leaning on the 10-year and 30-year Treasury yields via a bond buyback program, positioning himself as an increasingly activist market participant.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: Growing Treasury intervention in rates and FX is a policy trend to track for its knock-on effects on the dollar and precious metals.
insights.quote: Besson just got us kicked off uh fresh off intervening in the yen. He's now leaning on the 10-year and the 30-year.

insights.claim: Bessent's roughly $4 billion Treasury bond buyback is financially trivial (joked to cover only about two hours of market impact) but functions as an early symbolic signal that the Treasury, not yet the Fed, is starting to step in to support the bond market.
insights.speaker: Jerry Jordan, guest
insights.so_what: Small, symbolic Treasury interventions today can be the leading edge of much larger future intervention — a signal worth tracking even when the dollar amount looks immaterial.
insights.quote: a four billion B dollar bond buyback is what's that? Two hours... It's a signal more than anything else.

insights.claim: Bessent is now effectively on the other side of 'the great Soros trade,' analogous to the Bank of England in 1992 — stuck defending yields with no real choice but to eventually let stocks roll over (triggering a rate reprieve) or print more money and let the dollar weaken further; something has to give.
insights.speaker: Jerry Jordan, guest
insights.so_what: Frames the coming policy endgame as binary: an equity-market rollover that forces rates lower, or continued dollar debasement — both scenarios reinforce the case for gold.
insights.quote: He's now the Bank of England and he's stuck because they don't have a choice. They're going to have to either let it go and just let the markets figure it out.

insights.claim: Rejects 'inflation' as a distinct standalone phenomenon, arguing persistent price rises are really commodity price increases plus currency depreciation; expects an AI-driven 'jobs apocalypse' to weigh on wages even as commodity prices hold a higher structural floor than before (e.g., beef prices won't fully revert).
insights.speaker: Jerry Jordan, guest
insights.so_what: Reframes the inflation debate around commodity/currency dynamics rather than CPI — implies AI-driven wage weakness alongside a firmer commodity price floor rather than classic CPI-driven inflation.
insights.quote: I don't believe in inflation. I don't think it exists. I don't think it's actually a thing. I think what you have is you have commodity price increases or decreases and you have currency increases or decreases.

insights.claim: Expects continued dollar weakness as the U.S. government is forced to get more involved in supporting markets (money printing, rate caps), which should be structurally supportive of both gold and Bitcoin, even though Bitcoin's current trading drivers are unclear.
insights.speaker: Jerry Jordan, guest
insights.so_what: Positions both gold and Bitcoin as beneficiaries of an expected dollar-debasement policy path, though with lower conviction on the Bitcoin linkage specifically.
insights.quote: I think what we're looking at here is a weaker currency because the US government's going to have to get more involved. Um, and that's should be good for pre good for precious metals. I think it's good for Bitcoin.

themes.theme: Gold & Precious Metals: The Under-Owned Asset

insights.claim: Gold is up 6% year-to-date and 14% over the most recent quarter, coinciding with a resurgent 'debasement trade' narrative as the dollar weakens and Bitcoin re-enters an uptrend.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: Gold's quarterly acceleration alongside dollar weakness and a Bitcoin uptrend is consistent with a broad debasement-trade re-acceleration worth tracking as a regime signal.
insights.quote: gold's up 6% though year to date. I mean 6% year to date, 14% on the quarter.

insights.claim: Predicts that gold can outperform the stock market over the next three to five years, potentially behaving with roughly a beta of two to the S&P, driven by the expectation that policymakers will be forced into money printing, yield curve control, or rate caps to defend the bond market.
insights.speaker: Jerry Jordan, guest
insights.so_what: A high-conviction long-gold-vs-equities relative-value call explicitly tied to an expected yield-curve-control policy path, not just generic inflation hedging.
insights.quote: it's my prediction that you can own gold and outperform the stock market over the next three to five years. So, and now it may have a beta of two to the S&P.

insights.claim: Draws a direct historical parallel to the 1940s-50s U.S. interest rate caps, which he says unlocked the inflation that emerged in the 1960s-70s, a period during which gold steadily climbed — and sees a similar policy setup (forced rate suppression) forming today.
insights.speaker: Jerry Jordan, guest
insights.so_what: If policymakers repeat 1940s-50s style rate suppression, history suggests a multi-decade gold bull market could follow, as it did after that earlier episode.
insights.quote: we did this in the 1940s and 50s. We capped interest rates and we did it for a long time and that's what sort of unlocked the the inflation genie that we saw rear its head in 60s and 70s and gold just sort of crawled its way up during that whole period.

insights.claim: Precious metals remain dramatically under-owned — roughly 1% of a typical developed-market portfolio, dwarfed by central bank holdings — meaning even a small reallocation (e.g., trimming a 40% tech weighting to 39%) would represent a disproportionately massive flow into the comparatively tiny physical gold market.
insights.speaker: Jerry Jordan, guest
insights.so_what: Because the physical gold market is so small relative to paper/equity markets, only a modest portfolio reallocation shift is needed to move gold prices dramatically — a key reason for the high-conviction gold call.
insights.quote: if you're afraid of the paper markets and you try to pour the paper markets into the physical gold market or into the gold market, I mean, you're pouring the ocean into a thimble.

insights.claim: Distinguishes the current gold call from a 1970s-style stagflation replay — not forecasting 17% interest rates; notes that over a 200-year history the high on the 10-year has generally been around 6-7%, and believes roughly 7% would 'break everything' given today's much higher system-wide leverage.
insights.speaker: Jerry Jordan, guest
insights.so_what: Sets an implicit ceiling (~6-7% on the 10-year) beyond which the current highly-levered system would break, capping how far the 'higher for longer' scenario can realistically run before policy intervention becomes forced.
insights.quote: if you look at a 200 year history of interest rates, you know, the high is generally around six or 7%... I don't think we go much further because at 7% everything breaks everything.

insights.claim: A new structural feature versus the 1970s gold bull market is the availability of 2x/3x leveraged gold ETFs today, which didn't exist then and could make a crowded rush into gold considerably more volatile this cycle.
insights.speaker: Brooks Cutright, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Expect higher realized volatility in any future gold rally than in the 1970s precedent, due to leveraged-ETF amplification of retail flows.
insights.quote: the idea that when you're talking about everybody piling into golden all at the same time... it's going to be way more entertaining now with their 2x and 3x lever ETF.

themes.theme: Energy & Commodities: A Supply Squeeze Nobody's Pricing

insights.claim: Energy is the best-performing S&P 500 sector year-to-date, yet at under 4% of the index weighting it remains a marginal position size in most portfolios despite the outperformance.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: Energy's sector-leading YTD returns have not yet translated into meaningful portfolio ownership, leaving room for further inflows if the trend persists.
insights.quote: the best sector year to date is energy. I mean under it's under 4% of the index.

insights.claim: The market has largely shrugged off what is described as the biggest disruption to energy supply in a generation because elevated inventories have cushioned the immediate impact; the worst-case outcome for the energy market would be oil spiking to $150.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: A supply disruption currently masked by inventory buffers could reprice sharply once those buffers are exhausted, with $150 oil as the tail-risk marker to watch.
insights.quote: the worst thing that can happen in the energy markets is that oil goes to 150.

insights.claim: Oil storage drawdowns have reached unprecedented levels via both floating storage and SPR releases, combined with reduced buying (including from China), even as the outright oil price has remained range-bound rather than spiking.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: Large, historically unusual inventory drawdowns without a corresponding price spike suggest latent supply tightness that could surface abruptly once storage buffers run out.
insights.quote: we've never seen this level of of storage draw down between floating storage... We've drawn 140 billion I think uh barrels down of floating storage another 300 through SPRs um and lack of buying.

insights.claim: Citing commodity strategist Jeff Currie, crack spreads (refining margins for gasoline, diesel and jet fuel) are near all-time highs while crude itself stays range-bound; if refineries restart and crack spreads compress, oil itself could then rise as refinery demand for crude increases — a 'heads I lose, tails I lose' setup underpinning a secular commodity bull case.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: Either outcome (crack-spread compression via refinery restarts, or continued crack-spread strength) points toward higher crude demand and price support, reinforcing a bullish energy/commodity stance.
insights.quote: maybe what'll happen is the refineries will get themselves back up and running and so the crack spreads will come will come down but oil will go up because now the demand for oil goes up.

insights.claim: Rising gasoline and diesel prices are already flowing through to consumer spending, evidenced by Walmart's cautious consumer commentary and tariff pass-through concerns, alongside a recent weak stretch for restaurant stocks outside of apparent short-covering rallies.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: Energy cost pass-through to the consumer is an early, real-time signal worth tracking via retail and restaurant commentary/pricing ahead of broader CPI data.
insights.quote: Walmart gave us a pretty sober consumer read. But the interesting story there I thought was their comments on tariff pass through and what that could mean for inflation.

insights.claim: Private equity firms have used insurance-company float (ultimately funded by mom-and-pop annuity holders) to finance opaque investments over roughly the past eight years, with recent stress signals — including an LA Lakers ownership fire sale and reported solvency issues at Phoenix Suns owner Matt Ishbia — flagged as possible early warning signs of a hidden systemic risk.
insights.speaker: Jerry Jordan, guest
insights.so_what: PE-linked insurance leverage is a potential hidden systemic risk to monitor via unusual liquidity events among PE-connected owners/sponsors, not just headline insurer financials.
insights.quote: you don't know who's swimming naked till the tide goes out. And the insurance companies are now enormous. And we can't let them fail.

insights.claim: Private equity has steadily acquired insurance companies over the past 8-10 years, effectively exploiting the fact that PE sponsors themselves won't be bailed out but the retail policyholders behind their insurance float will be, which has changed the underlying risk-taking incentives ('game theory') in the insurance industry.
insights.speaker: Brooks Cutright, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: PE ownership of insurers may be encouraging riskier investment behavior than the underlying float would otherwise support, since downside is implicitly backstopped by policyholder protection.
insights.quote: it is borderline alarming when you look through the acquisitions of insurance companies over the past 8 to 10 years of who's actually been buying them... Private equity won't get bailed out, but our customers will.

insights.claim: Because the insurance sector is effectively too big to fail (it protects retail annuity holders), any stress event there implies further government money-printing or bailout risk ahead, reinforcing the broader dollar-debasement and gold thesis.
insights.speaker: Jerry Jordan, guest
insights.so_what: An insurance-sector stress event would likely trigger further monetary intervention, adding another catalyst pathway (beyond bond-market defense) toward continued dollar weakness and gold strength.
insights.quote: they put the risk in grandma's annuity. They... can't screw grandma and so so they're gonna have to bail him out. And so there's more money printing regardless.

insights.claim: A recent industry survey found 56% of insurance companies still plan to direct their next marginal investment dollar into direct credit, underscoring how central insurers remain as a source of demand for private/direct credit markets.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: Continued heavy insurer allocation to direct credit means the sector's health remains structurally tied to private credit market conditions, a channel worth watching for contagion risk.
insights.quote: 56% still want to put it in direct credit of course because that's what they're supposed to be doing.
